rows.textLatex: Why buffers are used at the input side of PLA?
rows.solution: A PLA input buffer draws little current from the external input source and drives the internal AND plane with a stronger output. Each buffer provides both polarities, $A$ and $\overline A$, so a product term can use either literal without adding an external inverter. Figure 17 shows this true/complement output pair.

note_ref.section: Input Buffer

rows.textLatex: Name different switching techniques employed in configurable hardware.
rows.solution:
The notes summarize these configurable-switch technologies in Fig. 49.

| Technology | How it programs the connection | Retention |
|---|---|---|
| Fuse | Opens a conducting link permanently. | Nonvolatile, one-time programmable |
| Antifuse | Makes a permanent connection through a previously insulating link. | Nonvolatile, one-time programmable |
| EPROM | Floating-gate storage controls the switch; the device can be erased with UV and reprogrammed. | Nonvolatile |
| EEPROM | Electrically erasable storage controls the switch. | Nonvolatile, electrically reprogrammable |
| SRAM | A stored bit controls a pass gate or multiplexer. | Volatile, reload on power-up |

note_ref.section: Programmable memory links and FPGA switching technologies
note_ref.verified_diagram: Figs. 13 and 47–49, pass-gate control, antifuses and the technology summary.

rows.textLatex: 'Out of Board Programming is always desired compared to In-System Programming'- Justify in favour of or against the statement.
rows.solution:
The statement is false. **In-system programming (ISP)** configures a supported device while it stays on its target board, for example through the JTAG connection shown in Fig. 45. It avoids removing a large, fragile package and buying a programming socket. The CAD tools produce configuration bits for the completed design. ISP is useful for prototypes and later updates.

**Out-of-board programming** can still be appropriate when the device lacks ISP support or when parts must be programmed and verified before assembly. The choice depends on the device and manufacturing process.

note_ref.section: Programming a CPLD, reasons for employing ISP and design download

rows.textLatex: How can ROM be used as PLD?
rows.solution:
Treat the $p$ input variables as address bits and each of the $N$ logic functions as one ROM data output. Program each address with the $N$-bit word specified by the truth table. A full ROM uses $2^p$ words of $N$ bits. The fixed address decoder selects one minterm and the stored bits specify which outputs are true for it.

```text
p input bits → address decoder → selected ROM word → N logic outputs
```

Example: for $F=A\oplus B$, store `0, 1, 1, 0` at addresses `00, 01, 10, 11`. This is the one-output version of the ROM block in Fig. 15.

note_ref.section: Stored truth table and ROM as a PLD
note_ref.verified_diagram: Fig. 15, ROM with address inputs and data outputs.

rows.textLatex: Distinguish between SPLDs and CPLDs.
rows.solution:
| Feature | SPLD | CPLD |
|---|---|---|
| Organization | One small programmable structure such as a PAL or PLA. | Several SPLD-like logic blocks connected by programmable interconnect. |
| Capacity | Fewer I/O pins, product terms and macrocells. | More resources for larger functions, with additional routing options and more flexible macrocells. |
| Example | PAL 16R8 or 22V10. | Altera MAX 7000, with LABs and a programmable interconnect array. |

The notes describe many CPLDs as EEPROM-based, but the underlying memory technology does not by itself distinguish an SPLD from a CPLD.

note_ref.section: SPLD examples and Altera CPLD organization

rows.textLatex: What is an ASIC?
rows.solution: An **application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC)** is an IC designed and fabricated for a particular application or class of applications. A foundry manufactures the circuit to the design specification. An ASIC can reduce board area and power, and it can have a low unit cost in high-volume production. It has a high up-front design and verification cost. A hardware redesign can require another fabrication run.

note_ref.section: ASIC features, advantages and disadvantages

rows.textLatex: What are the different logic states available in VHDL as per IEEE standard?
rows.solution:
IEEE 1164 defines nine values in `std_ulogic` and its resolved subtype `std_logic`.

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `'U'` | Uninitialized |
| `'X'` | Forcing unknown |
| `'0'` | Forcing low |
| `'1'` | Forcing high |
| `'Z'` | High impedance |
| `'W'` | Weak unknown |
| `'L'` | Weak low |
| `'H'` | Weak high |
| `'-'` | Don't care |

note_ref.section: The std_logic type and the IEEE 1164 resolution table

rows.textLatex: Explain with proper circuit diagram, how a single macrocell can be used to implement various outputs.
rows.solution:
The macrocell in Fig. 38 takes an OR-plane sum $S$ and feeds it to both a D flip-flop and a bypass path. Two fuse-controlled multiplexers select the source and its polarity. An intact fuse holds the respective select at 0. With the fuse open, the pull-up makes the select 1.

```text
                  ┌── D flip-flop ── Q ── [0] ┐
OR-plane sum S ───┤                           MUX S1 ── T ──┬─ [0] ┐
                  └── bypass S ────────── [1] ┘              └─ NOT → [1] → MUX S0 → buffer → pin
                                                  Selected feedback → AND-plane input buffer
```

| S1 fuse | S0 fuse | Pin value when enabled |
|---|---|---|
| Intact | Intact | $\overline Q$ |
| Intact | Open | $Q$ |
| Open | Intact | $\overline S$ |
| Open | Open | $S$ |

These are the four Fig. 39 configurations. In the schematic, the final inversion comes from the output buffer, so the direct MUX branch gives an inverted pin value. The flip-flop gives registered operation and the bypass gives combinational operation. The output-enable term controls the three-state driver. The feedback multiplexer selects the complemented register output or the pin-side signal. That selected signal then passes through the feedback inverter shown in Fig. 38.

note_ref.section: Sample macrocell and four fuse configurations
note_ref.verified_diagram: Fig. 38 and Fig. 39(a–d), registered/bypass and polarity selection.

rows.textLatex: Describe the structure and functionality of SRAM cell with proper diagram.
rows.solution:
Fig. 11 uses a cross-coupled MOS latch to store one bit as complementary internal nodes $D$ and $\overline D$. Positive feedback keeps the stored value while power is supplied. The addressing and read/write transistors connect the latch to the appropriate data lines.

```text
                      ┌── cross-coupled MOS latch ──┐
Data in → T9 → T7 → T5 → D                     D̅ → T6 → T8 → T10 → Data out (complement)
          W    Ay   Ax                               Ax   Ay    R
```

- **Hold.** With the cell disconnected, the latch retains its bit while powered.
- **Write.** Set `W=1`, `Ay=1`, `Ax=1`. The input reaches the latch through T9, T7 and T5.
- **Read.** Set `R=1`, `Ay=1`, `Ax=1`. The complementary value is available through T6, T8 and T10 and can be inverted if the true output is required.
- **Use in a PLD.** The stored configuration bit controls a pass gate between routing segments. A stored 0 leaves the path at high resistance. SRAM is volatile, so a design needs configuration after power-up.

note_ref.section: Static MOS RAM cell and configuration use
note_ref.verified_diagram: Figs. 11–14, storage cell, control lines and pass-gate use.

rows.textLatex: Illustrate with relevant circuits the operation of a PAL device.
rows.solution:
### PAL architecture

```text
Inputs → Input buffers → Programmable AND plane
         (I and NOT I)       │ product terms
                             ▼
                         Fixed OR plane → Output buffer → Outputs
                             │
                             └─ Optional register or feedback to AND plane
```

**Input buffers.** Each external input supplies both its true and complemented values to the AND plane.

**Programmable AND plane.** Select the input literals for each product term by retaining the required connections and opening the others. For example, a term that retains $A$ and $\overline B$ realizes $A\overline B$. With $M$ inputs and $n$ product terms, the array has $2Mn$ possible fusible connections.

**Fixed OR plane.** Each OR gate receives a predetermined subset of the product terms. Thus each output is a sum of its assigned terms. The groups of fixed connections are shown by solid dots in Fig. 35.

**Output and feedback.** A buffer drives the output pin. A registered PAL can feed an OR output through a flip-flop. Depending on the device, an output can return to the AND plane, with optional inversion, for use in another product term. Fig. 36 shows this feedback arrangement.

Example: retain the links for $A,\overline B$ in one AND column, and $B,C$ in another. If the fixed OR gate receives those two columns, it produces $Y=A\overline B+BC$. Opening a literal link removes that literal from the product. The figure distinguishes the programmable AND links from the fixed OR links.

note_ref.section: Programmable Array Logic (PAL) as PLD
note_ref.verified_diagram: Fig. 35 (AND and OR planes) and Fig. 36 (feedback and register). Diagram simplified from the notes.

rows.textLatex: Draw neatly an OR matrix and show how different minterms can be ORed.
rows.solution:
An OR plane has product terms on its columns and output sums on its rows. In Figs. 23–26, each available crosspoint is a transistor path with a programmable link. A high product term whose link is intact pulls the corresponding sum line high. An open link removes that term from the sum. The pull-down returns an undriven row to 0.

```text
             product-term inputs
              m0   m1   m2   m3
Y0 (OR row)    ×    ·    ×    ·
Y1 (OR row)    ·    ×    ×    ×

× = intact/programmed link    · = open link
```

Thus $Y_0=m_0+m_2$ and $Y_1=m_1+m_2+m_3$. The matrix uses minterms as inputs in this example. A PLA can also feed it minimized product terms.

note_ref.section: OR matrix operation and compact notation
note_ref.verified_diagram: Figs. 23–26, transistor OR plane and crosspoint representation.

rows.textLatex: Describe with neat circuit diagram, the functionality of a commercially available FPGA chip.
rows.solution:
**Example: Xilinx XC4000.** The SRAM-based FPGA contains an array of configurable logic blocks (CLBs), peripheral I/O blocks and horizontal/vertical routing channels. Configuration bits set LUT contents and programmable connections. On power-up an SRAM-based device needs the configuration loaded again.

```text
I/O blocks ↔ programmable channel switches ↔ CLB array ↔ I/O blocks
                short / medium / long routing wires

Inside one XC4000 CLB (simplified from Fig. 65)
F1–F4 → LUT F ───┬─→ local output or register
                  ├─→ LUT H → combined output or register
G1–G4 → LUT G ───┘      ↑ S1
                    two flip-flops available
```

The two four-input LUTs implement arbitrary four-input Boolean functions independently. The third LUT combines the F and G outputs with another input when required. For example, a two-input XOR is made by loading the XOR truth-table bits into a LUT and ignoring its unused inputs. Flip-flops support sequential outputs. Programmable switches connect block pins to tracks and join selected tracks. The fitter chooses routes, which influences propagation delay. The notes also describe fast carry hardware for arithmetic.

note_ref.section: Xilinx XC4000 CLB, LUTs, carry logic and programmable routing
note_ref.verified_diagram: Figs. 65–66, XC4000 CLB and wire segments.

rows.topic: PLA Implementation of 3-Bit Odd Parity Generator
rows.textLatex: Develop and show the programmed structure of a PLA implementing an odd parity generator of 3-bit input.
rows.solution:
For an odd-parity generator, the parity bit makes the total number of 1s in the four-bit transmitted word odd. Thus $P=1$ when the three data bits contain an even number of 1s.

$$P=\overline{A\oplus B\oplus C}=\overline A\,\overline B\,\overline C+\overline A BC+A\overline BC+AB\overline C=\sum m(0,3,5,6).$$

| ABC | P | ABC | P |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| 000 | 1 | 100 | 0 |
| 001 | 0 | 101 | 1 |
| 010 | 0 | 110 | 1 |
| 011 | 1 | 111 | 0 |

```text
                 programmable AND plane          OR plane
                 A A̅   B B̅   C C̅                to P
m0               · ×   · ×   · ×                  ×
m3               · ×   × ·   × ·                  ×
m5               × ·   · ×   × ·                  ×
m6               × ·   × ·   · ×                  ×

× = connection present     · = open
```

This adapts the notes' PLA full-adder layout. The full-adder sum output is the detector for an odd number of input 1s. Inverting that output gives the odd-parity **bit** required here.

note_ref.section: PLA input literals, AND/OR matrix and full-adder worked example, adapted to generate an odd-parity bit

rows.textLatex: Harvard architecture and Princeton architecture
rows.solution:
| Feature | Harvard | Princeton (Von Neumann) |
|---|---|---|
| Instruction/data storage | Separate program and data spaces. | Shared address space and memory. |
| CPU connection | Separate instruction and data paths. | Shared transfer path. |
| Access | An instruction fetch and data access can occur concurrently. | They compete for the shared path in the simplified architecture. |
| Example | AVR uses separate program Flash and data space. | A basic stored-program computer with a single common memory. |

```text
Harvard:   program memory ←→ CPU ←→ data memory
Princeton: program + data memory ←→ CPU
```

note_ref.section: Princeton and Harvard organization and the AVR example
note_ref.verified_diagram: The separate and shared bus diagrams on pp. 34–35.

rows.textLatex: Volatile memory and Non-volatile memory
rows.solution:
| Feature | Volatile memory | Nonvolatile memory |
|---|---|---|
| Power removed | Loses stored contents. | Retains stored contents. |
| Examples | SRAM and DRAM. | ROM, EEPROM and Flash. |
| Typical use in AVR | SRAM holds live data, variables and the stack. | Flash stores instructions and EEPROM retains settings. |

Ordinary SRAM needs no periodic refresh while powered. DRAM needs refresh even while it is powered. Both are volatile.

note_ref.section: ROM, EEPROM, Flash and read/write memory families

rows.textLatex: RISC and CISC technology of processing
rows.solution:
| Feature | RISC | CISC |
|---|---|---|
| Instruction design | Emphasizes simple operations and fairly regular encodings. | Offers more complex instructions, often with several addressing or encoding forms. |
| Memory access | Commonly uses explicit load/store instructions, with arithmetic on registers. | Some instructions can operate directly on memory operands. |
| Implementation | Simple instruction forms help decoding and pipelining. | A single instruction may combine operations that need several simpler instructions. |
| Example | AVR. | x86. |

Instruction count alone does not determine execution time. The clocks per instruction, clock period and actual instruction sequence also matter.

note_ref.section: RISC and CISC comparison and AVR architecture example

rows.textLatex: What are the name of registers associated with on-chip timers and counters? How do they control operations of timer and counter? Explain with appropriate bit format of registers and functionality of each of the bits in an organized manner.
rows.solution:
Use **16-bit Timer/Counter1** as the example from the notes. Other timers have analogous registers with width and channel differences.

```text
bits       7       6       5       4       3       2       1       0
TCCR1A    COM1A1  COM1A0  COM1B1  COM1B0  COM1C1  COM1C0  WGM11   WGM10
TCCR1B    ICNC1   ICES1   —       WGM13   WGM12   CS12    CS11    CS10
TCCR1C    FOC1A   FOC1B   FOC1C   —       —       —       —       —
TIFR1     —       —       ICF1    —       OCF1C   OCF1B   OCF1A   TOV1
TIMSK1    —       —       ICIE1   —       OCIE1C  OCIE1B  OCIE1A  TOIE1
```

- `TCCR1A`: each `COM` pair controls the action of its `OC1A/B/C` pin on compare. `WGM11:10` and `WGM13:12` together select the waveform/counting mode, such as Normal, CTC or PWM.
- `TCCR1B`: `ICNC1` enables the input-capture noise filter and `ICES1` selects the capture edge. `CS12:10 = 000` stops the timer. `001`–`101` select internal clock divisions 1, 8, 64, 256, 1024. `110` or `111` selects falling or rising edges at external `T1`, respectively.
- `TCCR1C`: writing 1 to a `FOC` strobe forces the respective compare-output action in a non-PWM mode.
- `TCNT1` holds the live count. `OCR1A/B/C` are compare values and `ICR1` captures the count on the configured edge. Some modes also use `OCR1A` or `ICR1` as TOP.
- `TIFR1`: `ICF1` signals capture, `OCF1A/B/C` signal compare events, and `TOV1` signals overflow or the mode-specific rollover event. Write 1 directly to the relevant flag bit to clear it. `TIMSK1` enables the respective interrupt requests and the global `I` bit must also be set to enter an ISR.

note_ref.section: Timer/counter schematic, Timer1 control and flag registers, CTC and external clocking
note_ref.verified_diagram: 16-bit Timer1 control and flag bit rows.

note_refs.section: 16-bit Timer/Counter compare path and interrupt enable bits

rows.textLatex: Explain the functionality of Data Direction Register (DDR) and Port Input Register (PIN) with appropriate circuit diagram.
rows.solution:
Each I/O pin has a `DDRx` direction bit, a `PORTx` latch bit, and a `PINx` read bit. `DDRx[n]=1` enables the output driver and the `PORTx[n]` latch drives the pin. `DDRx[n]=0` disables that driver, and software reads the pin level from `PINx[n]`. With the pin configured as input, setting `PORTx[n]` enables its pull-up when global pull-ups are enabled. Clearing it leaves the input high impedance.

```text
                      DDRx[n] → output enable
                                       │
PORTx[n] output latch ───────────→ [driver] ───●── Px.n
                                               │
     VCC ─ optional weak pull-up ──────────────┤
                                               └── [input buffer] → PINx[n] read
```

On the ATmega2560, writing a one to `PINx[n]` toggles the corresponding `PORTx` latch. Ordinary input sampling just reads `PINx`.

note_ref.section: DDR, PORT and PIN functions and masked register operations
note_ref.verified_diagram: Port direction and read/write paths on pp. 20–23.

rows.textLatex:
Write short note on:
Flags of timer and counter
rows.solution:
`TIFRn` stores timer event flags. Using a 16-bit timer such as Timer1, its bit order from bit 7 to bit 0 is `— — ICF1 — OCF1C OCF1B OCF1A TOV1`.

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `TOVn` | Overflow or the rollover specified by the selected waveform mode. In Normal mode a 16-bit count goes from `0xFFFF` to zero. |
| `OCFnA/B/C` | The live counter matches the channel's output-compare value. Only channels implemented by that timer are present. |
| `ICFn` | An input-capture event has copied the counter value into `ICRn` on a timer with capture hardware. |

The flags can be polled even when their interrupts are masked. To acknowledge a polled compare-A event, write only its mask with `TIFR1 = _BV(OCF1A);`. An ISR requires the corresponding `TIMSKn` enable and the global interrupt bit. Hardware clears the corresponding flag when it executes that interrupt vector. Avoid rewriting other flag bits when clearing one.

note_ref.section: TIFR bit layout, overflow flag and compare flag
